Presidential Ramblings
By Don Gamble
As I begin my term as President, I want to express
my deep appreciation to Steve Hansen for his leadership over the past four years. Steve guided the
Guild with steadiness, generosity, and a genuine
commitment to helping our community thrive. His
work has strengthened the foundation we all stand
on, and I’m grateful for the care and clarity he
brought to the role.
I also want to acknowledge the newly elected
members of the Board. We have a strong, engaged
group this year, a Board eager to build a Guild we
can all be proud of and to support an exciting, energized program for the year ahead. Their commitment and enthusiasm are already shaping the work
we’re doing behind the scenes, and I’m looking forward to what we’ll accomplish together.
One of the things I’m most excited about is our ongoing lineup of visiting demonstrators and handson workshops. This season, we welcome Matt
Monaco, with more exceptional turners already
being lined up. Our goal is to host three visiting demonstrators each season, giving members regular
opportunities to learn from some of the best in the
craft. Every time I attend a demo or workshop, I
come away with something new, even when I’m
convinced I won’t. Those small insights accumulate,
and over time, they’ve made me a better turner. I
know many of you have had the same experience.
I’m also pleased to share that Focus on Form and
Finish (FoFF) returns to our March meeting after a
long absence. This 30-minute, in-person session
begins at 6:30 pm, just before the regular Guild
meeting. FoFF will not be streamed online; it is
meant to be a hands-on, in-the-room conversation.
Larry Stevenson will guide participants through a
thoughtful discussion of the pieces we turn, helping
us look more deeply into form, proportion, detail,
and intention. Bring your questions, bring a piece if
you’d like, and come ready to share your thoughts
and learn from others. And if you haven’t already,
make sure you’ve joined the FoFF online interest
group, where the conversation continues between
meetings.
Right behind FoFF, we’re developing Focus on
Learning and Sharing (FoLS). Ed Pretty is shaping
this into a 30-minute, pre-meeting, in-person session where members can share skills, techniques,
and small insights that don’t require a full demo
slot. These will be short, informal 5-10-minute micro-demos, the kind of practical tips that help all of
us improve. For example, someone might show
new turners how to cut a clean, well-formed tenon,
or demonstrate how to make a controlled pull cut
without getting a catch. These small, focused
demonstrations are a great way to learn from one
another in a relaxed, back-of-the-hall setting. Keep
an eye out for more details, and be sure to sign up
for the FoLS online interest group so you don’t
miss the launch.
As we look ahead, two of our core operational
teams are seeking additional support. The Visiting
Demonstrator Team plays a central role in bringing
world-class turners to our Guild. Art Liestman will
continue as the Visiting Demonstrator Advisor, and
Pippa Lattey is joining the team. After many years
of exceptional service, Dustin Cook is taking a wellearned breather. Dustin has been instrumental in
shaping our demonstrator program, and we owe
him a sincere thank you for his dedication and the
countless hours he has invested. As we refine and
clarify the responsibilities of this team, we are looking for additional volunteers to be part of this important work (see Pippa Lattey).
Our Materials Coordinator team is also looking to
build more depth so we can continue providing the
materials needed to offer our visiting demonstrator demos, workshops, and intro classes. This is a
hands-on, practical area where extra help makes a
real difference (see Lucas Siba).
The Class Turning Coordinator is a coordination
role, not an instructor role, ensuring our Intro to
Turning classes happen smoothly. Peter Hill is com-
(Continued on page 4)

pleting his term in May, and we thank him for his
steady and important work (see Lucas Siba).
The Meeting Coordinator ensures the monthly
meeting room is set up and taken down, including
chairs, tables, and the safety screen. We have lots
of hands to help; this role ensures there is no lastminute scramble and that everything is ready when
members arrive (see Scott Morgan).
We are also looking for a New Member Liaison to
welcome new members and help them find their
footing
in
the
Guild
(see
Scott
Morgan).
The For Sale / Swap / Gift Group Leader coordinates our Swap Meet activities, the online forum,
and the monthly table at the back of the hall,
helping members exchange tools, wood, and
equipment in a safe and organized way (see Donna
Rhindress).
And the Sawdust Huddles Group Leader coordinates woodturner meet-ups outside of the Guild’s
regular activities, creating relaxed opportunities
for members to connect and share ideas, whether
that’s over coffee or as a small group visiting a
member’s shop (see Matt Lo).
We also had one Member-at-Large position open
this year, created when I moved into the President’s role. Ed Pretty has stepped forward to fill
that one-year term, and I want to thank him for
taking it on. Thoughtful contributions like his help
keep the Guild responsive, resilient, and moving
forward.
I’m also pleased to share that Simon Britchford has
stepped forward to take on the role of Newsletter
Editor. Simon brings fresh energy and exciting ideas for how we can continue to evolve the newsletter, and his first edition will be next month’s
newsletter. I want to extend a heartfelt thank you
to Steve Fairbairn for his incredible work over the
years. His dedication, consistency, and craftsmanship have shaped the newsletter into what it is today. Steve is now passing the torch to Simon, and
we’re grateful to both of them for their contributions.
If you’ve ever wondered how to get more involved,
or if you’re looking for a way to give back, there is
a place for you here. Whether you have an hour a
month or a few hours a week, your contribution
makes a meaningful difference.
This is your Guild. Together we make it stronger.
Together we learn more. And together we continue the tradition of sharing, teaching, and turning
that makes this hobby and community so special.
I’m looking forward to the year ahead, learning
with you, working alongside you, and celebrating
the craft we all love.
Don

Editor’s Notes
By Steve Fairbairn
I began publishing our guild’s newsletter in the
summer of 2020 and took over the role of editor in
May 2021. It has been an extremely rewarding
task working with some amazing members over the
years and I thank all of you, our readers, for tuning
in every month. I especially would like to thank
everyone who has submitted articles over the
years. A special thank you to Diana Dougherty for
wrangling the (mostly) monthly Member Profiles.
Since all good things eventually come to an end,
this will be my last GVWG Newsletter. I am passing
the reins of Editor/Publisher to Simon Britchford
starting with the April edition of our newsletter.
Simon brings a wealth of relevant experience and
has some exciting new ideas for the design of our
publication. I am very much looking forward to
reading Simon’s first newsletter in April.
Steve

When I started this series I was wanting to incorporate three things into the design. These are :
1. Quilting Designs
2. Metallic Finishes you see in Raku pottery
3. 3D Illusions that you see in MC Escher’s work
The problem became how to stretch a 2 dimensional design around a 3 dimensional object and
have it look correct It is essential that your design
start on a piece of paper. You will need a piece of
graph paper that will allow you to make designs
with relative ease with regards to the angles you
require. I found the easiest way to do this was
with Microsoft Excel. Create a blank spreadsheet
and configure printed borders for the cells. Adjust
the width and height of the cells so that the diagonal is the correct angle. It helps to hold a 30/60
triangle to the screen to get a good approximation
before printing a test sheet. When you get it correct save the file so that you didn’t have to do that
again.
Be careful in your designs. It is easy to make a mistake. I work in elements. To me an element is defined as the primary geometric shape in your design. Start at the top of the paper and include several elements so that you can see them interlock.
Check the height and width of each of the element.
With the Tumbling Blocks design the smallest cube
is 1 full division, so the larger cube must be 2 divisions. (In time this will become obvious but in the
beginning it can be frustrating. You need to do an
accurate count of how many divisions until the
pattern starts repeating itself, not just the individual element. With the “Inner City” design the
pattern repeats every 6 divisions whereas in the
“Tumbling Blocks”, it repeats every 4 divisions.
This is important because you need to draw vertical divisions onto your woodturning. I generally
choose 48 divisions because my lathe can index
easily into 48 segments or 96 divisions. 48 divisions is a multiple of 4 or 6. If your lathe doesn’t
have an indexing head that divides into however
many divisions you want, do not worry as there is
an easy solution. There are programs that allow
you to print a page with a radial design that you
specify how many divisions you want. Do a search
(Continued on page 6)
Layout of Geometric Designs - Notes from Larry
Stevenson’s February Meeting Demonstration
By Larry Stevenson

March 2026
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 6
on “radial graph maker program” and make your
choice.
Print out the radial design. Glue or tape it to a
piece of hardboard or plastic with a hole drilled in
it that you can place behind your chuck. Clamp an
upright onto the lathe bed (paint stirring stick) and
use a spring clamp to align with the marks on the
graph paper. Now you have a simple indexing
head.
Next is the task of dividing the turning into the required amount of divisions. I made a simple stick
that I am offering for 3 easy payments of $6.95 and
will it be customized to your lathe. Drill a hole suited for your pencil in a 2x2 at the correct height so
you are on centre of your lathe. The 2x2 has a
small piece of plywood screwed into the end
squarely to allow you to run this on the bed of your
lathe and allows you to scribe a parallel line down
the piece. I bandsaw a cut down through the 2x2
inline with the pencil and put a wood screw
through the 2x2 to tighten the pencil in place. The
pencil will need to be sharp as accuracy will matter
as you proceed. Index the head and repeat until
you have gone around the entire piece and have all
the divisions scribed.
Now comes the fun part. You need to scribe circumferential lines around the vessel that increase
in spacing as the diameter increases and then
eventually the spacing reduces as the diameter decreases. Go back to your drawings and look at the
angle that the diagonal leaves the horizontal reference line. For both of these examples it leaves at
30 degrees. Make yourself a flexible 30/60 triangle
from a piece of plastic from whatever you can find
it, an old yogurt lid, ice cream lid, duo-tang, etc. It
should be flexible and fairly small, maybe 4” on the
diagonal.
I should point out at this point that the wall thickness of your piece should be even as when you
cut away the excess wood you want the thickness
to look even. Lay this triangle onto the piece with
the x axis laying along the rim of the piece and intersect the diagonal from the 30 degree angle to
your next division line. Mark along the diagonal
where it intersects the next division. This completes your first circumferential division. Scribe
this division around your piece. Move the flexible
triangle to this new line and repeat. Be prepared
to spend some time doing this process. Laying out
the grid and the pattern can take the best part of 1
day especially when this is all new to you.
By looking at the picture, you can see that I have
only drawn in the chevrons. I have done so many of
these that when I am doing the pyrography I know
where the vertical lines go.
(Continued from page 5)
(Continued on page 7)
Marking Stick
Grid Layout on Demo Piece

March 2026
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 7
Now I use a device called a “Proportional Divider”.
I found some on ebay and purchased a set made by
Alvin. Set the pivot point wherever appropriate to
the angle you desire. I set one side of the divider
for the rise and the other for the run based on a
30/60 triangle. I still scribe in the circumferential
lines as I go. To check your work, draw a diagonal
line from the top between the intersections of the
grid. Only one line is necessary. You should see a
helical line. I draw these lines using the small plastic triangle, even to this day.
Take your time. Draw in the pattern on the piece. I
cannot stress enough to take time as making a mistake is extremely frustrating. This is supposed to be
fun and relaxing. I recommend that you stick with
each row and do one part of the design and go
around the piece. When you have gone around the
entire piece, switch to a different part of the design. I do the angular lines leaning one way and
then switch to the lines leaning the other direction.
Only do one row at a time. Mistakes are easy to
make and a pain to change. Once you have your
design drawn out on your piece, give yourself a pat
on the back. The hardest part is behind you. Take
a well deserved break.
The exacting process of pyrography comes next.
The burnt lines created by pyrography prevent the
dye that you colour the cells with, from bleeding
between the cells. Use a sharp straight edged pyrography pen to burn the lines in. Practice on a
scrap piece of the same species of wood to get the
correct temperature. You need the edge of the
pen to be sharp and clean so keep a soft brass
brush close by to clean the tip. You may need to
sharpen the edge with a diamond hone to ensure it
follows your lines as you burn them.
In the picture you will notice that I didn’t burn the
top outline. That is because I am going to remove
the wood that is not part of one of the geometrical
shapes. I do not want the corners of certain elements burnt.
Now that the burning is done you can cut out the
wood that is unwanted along the top edge of your
design, or the outer edge if you are doing a platter.
I use a micro-motor for this task with a small bit
called a “Mini Saw Drill Set 3/32” and 1/8” available from Woodcarver Supply. In the past I used an
(Continued from page 6)
(Continued on page 8)
Pattern Chevrons Only
Proportional Divider
No Burning On Top Outline

March 2026
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 8
air powered body saw that I purchased at KMS
tools. You will still need to use fine files and sandpaper stuck to popsicle sticks to clean up the edges. Once you have these cutouts cleaned up, you
need to burn the appropriate line in them to differentiate the elements in the design. This again prevents dye from flowing between the cells.
Go over the entire piece. Check all your lines and
ensure that the burning is complete. Finally sand
off all the pencil lines with a dual action sander going up to 240 or 280 grit. You do not want the
piece so smooth that the dye doesn’t want to penetrate the surface. Remove the nubbins on the
bottom and sand it smooth and sign the piece now
with an appropriate pyrography pen.
I now finish the inside of the piece with a matte
black acrylic paint. I do not want moisture in the
air affecting the finish on the exterior surface. You
may wonder “how do you reach around the corners to paint the underside?” I have modified two
brushes to allow me to reach inside and get to all
the interior areas. I use a light and a dental mirror
to ensure that all the areas are completely covered. Wait for it to dry and recheck the surface
with a light as little dots may appear where the
paint was stretched across a divot when wet. I
then do a second coat. The interior surface is now
complete.
Colour
Everyone has a personal way of colouring their
piece. This is my method and strategy. My strategy
is to enhance an illusion of 3 dimensions on a relatively flat surface. The materials I use are,
Prismacolor marks or Procion MX dye, metallic
acrylic paint, and interference pigment. I also use
Krylon Matte finish to protect the surface.
I imagine the sun or light coming from a certain
direction onto a 3 dimensional shape, thus creating
a light, medium and darker surface depending on
the angle that the light is hitting it.
On this piece I am showing you I used the
Prismacolor markers that I purchased from Curry’s
art supply in Toronto.
I have since switched to using Procion MX dyes as I
have more control over my choice of colours.
When applying the dyes I use a Holbein Water
Brush from Opus Art Supplies, Granville Island. It
is a Japanese hollow handled brush. You fill the
handle with dye solution and it is meant for water
colour painting. Be very careful and go sparingly.
Now dry brush the metallics.
(Continued from page 7)
(Continued on page 9)

This Month’s Cover - “Deep In The Woods”
By Don Gamble
This piece reflects that moment in the forest when
daylight is slipping away - the ground already dark,
the canopy still catching the last thin traces of sun.
The carved leaves echo those final glimmers you
can still see as you turn back toward home, aware
that night is coming fast and the familiar path is
fading into shadow.
“Deep in the Wood” holds that edge-of-light feeling - beautiful, uneasy, and charged with the
knowledge that darkness is close and the way out
may be longer than you hoped.
Maple • 4 3/4" x 2 3/4" • 3/16" thick • Finished
with acrylic paints
A dab of metallic the size of ½ a lentil is enough for
the entire piece. I then spray the piece with Krylon
Matte finish to protect the surface. I repeat dry
brushing on more metallic (sparingly) and finally
dry brush on the acrylic interference pigments
(again very sparingly). (Insert Picture Liquitex Interference Pigments) I have found that any finish over
the interference pigment effects its optical properties and I prefer it this way.
My suggestion to you is make some practice panels
to practice on. You need to get your strategy figured out before starting on your piece. Try different combinations of colour, metallic and interference paints and have a firm plan before starting
your piece. My way isn’t the gospel, only how I do
it. There are many methods and options and you
can discover your own voice and personalize your
work.

GVWG Kimberly Winkle Saturday Demo
By Brian Lunt
Kimberly presented a demonstration on creating a
three-legged stool using milk paint and detailed the
design process, emphasizing the importance of
considering material constraints and safety practices. She shared her background in ceramics and furniture design, highlighting how her training influenced her approach to woodturning. Kimberly explained the technical aspects of mortise and tenon
joinery, the importance of designing within material limitations, and the role of color in enhancing
design. She also discussed her philosophy on design, encouraging attendees to develop their skills
through observation and practice. She concluded
by demonstrating the turning process, focusing on
safety and proper technique.
Kimberly shared her experience learning about Manx
quilting, a unique folding fabric technique traditionally
developed on the Isle of Man
due to limited access to commodities. She explained that
Manx quilts feature pleated
fabric blocks arranged in log
cabin designs and are made
without batting, using materials like old clothes
and rugs. The technique was created to be simple
and require minimal tools, making it suitable for
use in low-light conditions.
Ceramics and Furniture Design Presentation
Kimberly presented her background in ceramics
and furniture design, highlighting her educational
journey and current role as a resident artist at the
Appalachian Center for Craft in Tennessee.
She shared examples
of her work, including
vessels, mirrors, and
sculptural pieces, emphasizing her use of
milk paint and drawing
on surfaces. Kimberly
discussed how her ceramics background influences
her approach to woodturning and furniture making, and she expressed gratitude for the support
she received from the woodturning community,
particularly from Nick Cook. The presentation concluded with Kimberly introducing a demonstration
on creating a three-legged stool, which was part of
her involvement in a master apprentice program in
Tennessee.
Circle Measurement and Mortise Techniques
Kimberly
demonstrated
techniques for measuring
and marking circles without using actual numbers,
including using a flexible
tape measure or paper
folded in thirds. She discussed mortise and tenon
dimensions
for
an
8quarter stool project, recommending a tenon diameter of 1 to 1.25 inches and explaining the decision
to use through-mortises rather than throughwedged tenons to allow for shaping on the top surface.
The discussion covered
the creation of a custom
jig for cutting angled mortises at 105 degrees, using a Forstner bit at 600800 RPM, and the importance of clamping the
workpiece securely during drilling. Finally, Kim
explained her design process using paper sketches
and templates, emphasizing the need to design
within material and skill limitations, and addressed
how to handle square shoulders in tenons through
a two-step drill process.
(Continued on page 11)

Woodworking Design Philosophy Discussion
Kimberly discussed design
philosophy and approaches, emphasizing the importance of careful observation and understanding
personal aesthetics. She
recommended
taking
drawing classes to develop
visual analysis skills and
suggested
keeping
a
sketchbook for collecting
inspiration. The discussion also covered color theory, particularly how color combinations affect perception and how to use complementary colors
effectively in woodworking projects.
Woodturning Stool Leg Demonstration
She demonstrated woodturning techniques for creating a stool leg, focusing on template creation for
multiple pieces and safety practices. She explained
the importance of working from general to specific
shapes and discussed design principles of unity versus variety in woodturning. The demonstration
covered roughing out the leg shape using a roughing gouge, creating a mortise for joinery, and marking locations for beads on the leg.
Woodturning Techniques and Tools
Kimberly demonstrated woodturning techniques,
focusing on spindle gouge usage and bead turning.
She explained her preferred grip technique and
cutting method, emphasizing the importance of
proper tool positioning and controlled cutting actions. The discussion included guidance on tenon
fitting, glue selection, and considerations for
painting, including the use of shellac as a sealant to
prevent tannin reactions with paint. She also addressed the challenges of creating mortises without a drill press and recommended investing in essential woodworking tools like a drill press, bandsaw, and grinder for optimal results.
Kimberly then discussed fitting a tenon and discussed how to improve the fit, noting that while
one fit was poor, the overall structure was still
sturdy.
Faceplate Turning Techniques Demonstration
Kimberly demonstrated faceplate turning techniques, explaining the differences from
spindle turning and emphasizing the importance of using appropriate tools and
cutting directions to avoid
tear-out. She discussed various options for creating mortises
without a drill press, including using devices like Portalign or Drill
Wizard. The demonstration included truing up a faceplate, creating
beads, and considering design elements like unity and variety in the
project.
Milk Paint Techniques Demonstration
Kimberly demonstrated milk paint techniques, explaining the proper preparation and application
process. She recommended using a 1:1 ratio of water to powder and mixing colors while wet rather
than in powder form. The discussion covered brush
selection, with Kim preferring soft foam brushes
for ease of use and synthetic bristle brushes for
(Continued from page 10)
(Continued on page 12)

better control. She emphasized the importance of applying multiple light coats rather
than heavy coats to avoid
drips and sags and demonstrated how to use a hair dryer
on low to speed up drying
time while avoiding overheating. The session included
a practical demonstration of
painting techniques on a lathe
and by hand, with Kim explaining how to create different
effects and the proper sequence for applying multiple colors.
Kimberly demonstrated techniques for working
with milk paint, including application methods, finish options, and troubleshooting common issues.
She
explained
that
milk paint requires a
finish coat for protection
and
discussed
various finish options
including wax, penetrating oils, and polyurethane. The discussion
covered
best
practices for different

with tannins and addressed storage and rehydration of milk paint. She also shared techniques for
creating texture and patterns using tools like wood
burners and leather stamps, while emphasizing the
importance of proper surface preparation and multiple coats for optimal results.
Woodturning Dimensional Effects Techniques
Kimberly demonstrated techniques for creating
dimensional effects in woodturning, including using
thin black coats to highlight volume and shape. She
explained the process of applying multiple paint
coats (demonstrating up to 12+ coats without issues) and using the lathe with an awl tip to create
thread-like patterns. She also discussed her work
setup, describing how she uses both university facilities
and
her
home
workshop,
and provided details about the Appalachian
Center
for Craft's educational
programs
including their BFA and community workshop
offerings.
3-Leg Stool Milk Paint Demonstration
Kim demonstrated the process of making a 3-leg stool
using milk paint, including
techniques
for
applying
washes, sanding, and burnishing with #4 super fine
steel wool. She explained
the importance of straining
paint before use and storing it in the refrigerator to
prolong its life. The demonstration included using different grits of sandpaper
and steel wool for surface preparation and finishing, as well as applying paste wax as a topcoat.
Kimberly emphasized the importance of building
up light coats of paint rather than heavy ones and
shared a technique learned from a student that
involved applying paint heavily and then sanding
through to create interesting textures.
2 Days of Classes at KMS
Kimberly demonstrated to 14 students on two days
the process of making candle sticks and cake
stands utilizing all the process she showed at the
Saturday demo

I attended the Kimberly Winkle demo on March 14,
2026. The late Dr. David sweet, an accomplished
wood turner, mentor, colleague and very dear
friend of mind introduced me to wood turning and
was instrumental in having me join the GVWG. David always advised that when attending a demonstration, come away with a nugget that you can use
in the future. My education and professional career were very deeply rooted in science. As such, I
was not well connected to the arts. My wood turning hobby was verry much centred on practical versus artistic. I had never considered the use of
paints on a turned piece however, the nugget I
gained from Ms. Winkle's demo was an opening to
the possibility of trying her milk paint techniques.
In fact, I have just ordered a selection of milk paints
and look forward to trying these techniques on a
project currently on my lathe that is nearing completion. So, a giant nugget was obtained, Dr. Sweet
would be proud!
Kind regards
Brian Andrews
Letter
By Brian Andrews
15% Discount for GVWG Members!
How to Qualify:
•Stop giving your phone number at the cashier
counter. (Will be hard because we have been
doing this for years).
•Only tell them you are with the GVWG or Greater
Vancouver Woodturners Guild.
•Either statement will link your purchase to your
new 15% discount.
If you give the cashier your phone number, you will
only get the store 5% non-guild price.
By saying GVWG instead you get 15% guild price
If you are buying something that needs a warranty,
you just give them your Name and Address and that
will go on the electronic file.
If the item you are buying has a flyer sale that is
better than the 15%, then you will automatically get
the better price.
Every purchase you make in the store by doing the
above process adds to our GVWG Credit account.
We use this credit account to buy KMS Gift certificate prizes and even bought our Laguna lathe for
Sapperton Hall with this credit account. By doing
this you are giving yourself a better discount and
helping the guild at the same time.
If you are an out of town guild member, all you
have to do is type in GVWG as the customer name
when buying, and type in your full name, address
etc. in the ship to and you will get the 15% discount.
The 15% is an average savings and is based on the
cost margins from that manufacturer. This does not
apply to published special flyer items.
If we all do this, we can even get up to a bigger discount level in future!

Safety Guidelines for Woodturning
You mostly turn alone so safety is YOUR responsibility
 Always wear safety goggles or safety
glasses that include side protectors.
Use a full face shield for bowl, vessel, or
any turning involving chucks and faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/
or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder and
wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting
wrenches, and knockout bars immediately after use. Never leave them in
place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose
clothing, jewelry, or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating parts
or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the
workpiece is solidly mounted with stout
screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws
as a minimum). Do not use dry wall or
deck screws.
 When turning between centres, be certain the workpiece is firmly mounted
between the headstock driving centre
and tailstock centre.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in
place.
 Check that all locking devices on the
tailstock and tool rest assembly (rest
and base) are tight before operating the
lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by
hand to make sure it clears the toolrest
and bed before turning the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind
and in front of the workpiece, they are
the most likely areas for a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of this zone when
turning on the lathe, keeping your hand
on the switch in case you need to turn
the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning it on. Use slower speeds
for larger diameters or rough pieces
and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the
lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always
stop the machine to verify why. As a
starting point, consult your operator’s
manual for recommended speeds for a
particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed
is compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock
(Continued on page 33)

Page 33
with cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets,
knots, irregular shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid these types
of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the
toolrest, holding the tool in a controlled
but comfortable manner. Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless it is securely
tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations.
An experienced woodturner is capable
of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning
turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before
sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing,
and keep your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check
for damaged parts, alignment, binding
of moving parts, and other conditions
that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better
and safer performance. Don’t force a
dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose
for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t
use a lathe in damp or wet locations.
Do not use in presence of flammable
liquids or gases, and always keep a fully
-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
 Stay alert. Watch what you are doing.
Pay close attention to unusual sounds
or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate machines
when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
 Guard against electric shock. Inspect
electric cords for damage. Avoid the
use of extension cords.
 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn power off. Don’t leave
lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
 Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially band and
chain saws. Learn and follow the safety
guidelines for this equipment.
For more information on woodturning
safety please visit the AAW’s Woodturning Safety webpage and GVWG Safety
webpage.
